---
title: "Tips & Hacks"
subtitle: "Optional shortcuts, and exactly what each one costs you"
---

::: {.callout-important}
## Nothing on this page is required

[Core Setup](setup.qmd) gives you a fully working connection on its own. What
follows removes friction — mostly the password prompts — by relaxing something.
Each hack states what it relaxes. Read that line before you paste the command.
:::

## At a glance

| Hack | What you gain | What you give up |
|---|---|---|
| [Auto-unlock the keyring](#auto-unlock) | No keyring prompt after login | Anyone with your unlocked user session can read the password |
| [Keyring under WSL2](#wsl-keyring) | `secret-tool` works at all in WSL | Your Linux login password sits in a `600` file |
| [Password inline](#inline-password) | Nothing to set up, ever | Plain-text password on disk and in `ps`. **Last resort.** |

---

## Stop the keyring prompting — auto-unlock at login {#auto-unlock}

**Relaxes:** the keyring's separate password. Your secrets become as safe as your
login session and no safer — which for a single-user laptop with disk encryption
is a reasonable place to land.

By default GNOME Keyring has its own master password, so `rdp-work` triggers an
"Unlock Keyring" dialog. If the keyring password is set to *the same string as
your Linux login password*, PAM unlocks it automatically when you log in and the
dialog disappears for good.

### On a fresh keyring

When `secret-tool store` first asks you to create a keyring password, simply
enter your Linux login password. Done — nothing else to configure.

### On an existing keyring

```bash
seahorse &   # install with: sudo apt install -y seahorse
```

In Seahorse: right-click **Login** under *Passwords* → **Change Password** →
enter the old keyring password, then set the new one to your Linux login
password.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Leaving the new password *empty* also stops the prompts, but stores your
secrets **unencrypted** on disk. Match your login password instead — same
convenience, real encryption at rest.
:::

Confirm PAM is wired up (it is by default on Ubuntu desktop):

```bash
grep -r pam_gnome_keyring /etc/pam.d/ | grep -E 'login|gdm'
```

---

## Make the keyring work under WSL2 {#wsl-keyring}

**Relaxes:** your Linux login password ends up in a file readable only by you.

WSL2 has no login session and no desktop, so there is no D-Bus session bus and
no running keyring daemon. `secret-tool` therefore fails with **"Cannot
autolaunch D-Bus without X11 $DISPLAY"**, or hangs waiting for a prompt that
can never appear.

### Once per terminal (no secrets on disk)

```bash
eval "$(dbus-launch --sh-syntax)"
gnome-keyring-daemon --unlock --replace --daemonize
# then type your keyring password and press Ctrl+D
```

Safe, but you repeat it in every new shell.

### Automatic, at the cost of one file

Put the unlock password in a locked-down file and let `.bashrc` do the work:

```bash
install -m 600 /dev/null ~/.keyring_pw
printf '%s' 'your-keyring-password' > ~/.keyring_pw
```

Then append to `~/.bashrc`:

```bash
# --- WSL2: start D-Bus and unlock the keyring on first shell ---
if grep -qi microsoft /proc/version; then
  if [ -z "$DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS" ]; then
    eval "$(dbus-launch --sh-syntax)"
  fi
  if ! pgrep -u "$USER" gnome-keyring-d >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    gnome-keyring-daemon --unlock --replace --daemonize < ~/.keyring_pw >/dev/null 2>&1
  fi
fi
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`~/.keyring_pw` is plain text. `chmod 600` keeps other Linux users out, but
anyone who can read your Windows user profile can read it, and it is **not**
protected by BitLocker unless your whole drive is encrypted. Weigh that against
how sensitive the Windows account is.

Never let this file into a repository — it is covered by this repo's
`.gitignore`, but check with `git status` before committing anyway.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
WSL2 alternative worth knowing: skip Linux entirely and use the **Windows
Remote Desktop app** on the host, which handles credentials natively. The Linux
route earns its keep when you want the same `rdp-work` muscle memory across
machines, or scripted access from inside WSL.
:::

---

## The blunt fallback — password in the command {#inline-password}

**Relaxes:** essentially everything. Read the warning in full.

If the keyring is fighting you and you need to get work done today, FreeRDP will
take the password directly:

```bash
alias rdp-work='xfreerdp /v:<ULMS_SERVER_IP> /u:<WINDOWS_USER> \
  /p:"YourPasswordHere" \
  /dynamic-resolution +clipboard /cert:ignore \
  /drive:share,$HOME/rdp_share'
```

::: {.callout-caution}
## What this actually exposes

1. **`~/.bashrc` is world-readable by default** (`644`) and is exactly the file
   people copy between machines, back up, and paste into help threads.
2. **The password appears in `ps aux`** while the session runs, visible to every
   user on the machine.
3. **It lands in `~/.bash_history`** the first time you type the command manually.
4. Any dotfiles repository will happily commit it.

If your institution's Windows account is the same one used for email, VPN, and
student records, treat this as unacceptable rather than merely untidy.
:::

### A less-bad version of the same idea

Keep the password out of `~/.bashrc` and out of your history, at least:

```bash
install -m 600 /dev/null ~/.rdp_pw
printf '%s' 'YourPasswordHere' > ~/.rdp_pw

# in ~/.bashrc:
alias rdp-work='xfreerdp /v:<ULMS_SERVER_IP> /u:<WINDOWS_USER> \
  /p:"$(cat ~/.rdp_pw)" \
  /dynamic-resolution +clipboard /cert:ignore \
  /drive:share,$HOME/rdp_share'
```

That fixes problems 1, 3, and 4 above. The password is still visible in `ps`
(problem 2) and still unencrypted on disk. It is a stepping stone, not a
destination — go back to [Step 3](setup.qmd#step-3) when you have ten minutes.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Cleaning up afterwards

Once the keyring works, remove the leftovers:

```bash
shred -u ~/.rdp_pw 2>/dev/null
history -d $(history | grep -n 'rdp-work' | cut -d: -f1 | tail -1) 2>/dev/null
```

And if a password ever reached a git repository, rotate it. Deleting the file in
a later commit does not remove it from history.
:::
